771.title: Why Bhishma couldn't answer
771.hook: Draupadi asks the elders to their faces, and the greatest of them can't answer
771.carry: ahara shuddhi: as the food, so the mind
771.howItsDone: Bhishma's 'the ways of dharma are subtle' is still debated, and the later story of his answer on the bed of arrows is told in homes and religious talks to teach ahara shuddhi: what we live on shapes the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday Draupadi sent the messenger back with a question: whom had Yudhishthira lost first, himself or her? Asking what dharma requires is dharma too.

This part of the story is hard, and i'll tell it plainly and with care. Duhshasana goes to the women's rooms. Draupadi tries to get away, and he seizes her by the hair and drags her into the assembly. The telling says she's in a single garment, and in distress. Here's what stands out about her, in a hall full of men who have just watched her gambled away. She doesn't only cry out. She argues.
screen: `A HARD SCENE, TOLD WITH CARE.` → `DRAGGED INTO THE HALL.` → `SHE ARGUES.`

segments.voice: She looks at the elders and asks how they can sit and watch this. Where has the dharma of these kings gone? Then, plainly: was I won, or not? Answer it. Bhishma answers, and he is the greatest knower of dharma in that hall. The ways of dharma are subtle, he says. One who has lost himself can't stake what belongs to another. And yet a wife, as the custom of the time held, is under her husband's authority. Holding both, he says he can't settle it. Draupadi answers him sharply: Yudhishthira was called to play by skilled, crooked players, and had no skill himself. How was that a free choice? The epic leaves Bhishma's failure hanging. Hindu families tell a later story to answer it, one that isn't in the epic's own text. Years on, Bhishma lies dying on a bed of arrows, teaching dharma beautifully, and Draupadi laughs. Where was all this wisdom in the hall? And he tells her: back then i was living on Duryodhana's food, and it clouded my mind. The arrows have drained that blood, and now i see clearly. That story carries a real Hindu teaching: ahara shuddhi, purity of what we take in. The Chandogya Upanishad says that when what we take in is pure, the mind becomes pure. Families say it simply: as the food, so the mind. It means more than what's on the plate. It means how the food was earned, and whose table you owe.
screen: `WAS I WON, OR NOT?` · `BHISHMA: DHARMA IS SUBTLE.` · `WAS IT A FREE CHOICE?` · `ON THE BED OF ARROWS: IT WAS THE FOOD.` · then, large: `AS THE FOOD, SO THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal or drink, pause for one breath and think about where it came from: who grew it, who earned it, who cooked it. Many Hindus say a short line before eating, like the Gita verse that begins brahmarpanam, offering the meal to God. If you pray, say it, or your own grace; if you don't, simply thank the hands behind the food.
Draupadi's question. She asked the elders to their faces, and Bhishma, who knew dharma best, called it subtle and couldn't answer.

772.title: Vikarna speaks for her
772.hook: Bhima answers with fire, Arjuna holds him back, and Vikarna, a Kaurava, answers with reasons
772.carry: dharma comes before your own side
772.tomorrow: What happens when they pull at her sari?
772.howItsDone: Vikarna is remembered in retellings as the Kaurava who spoke for Draupadi, held up beside Vibhishana as one who put dharma before his own side; Arjuna's restraint of Bhima is told as the brothers refusing to turn on each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday Draupadi's question met Bhishma's silence. In the story families tell, the food he lived on had clouded him. As the food, so the mind.

Two voices break the silence, and they break it in opposite directions. First Bhima. He has watched his eldest brother stake him, lose him, and then lose Draupadi, and his anger has nowhere to go. In the telling, he turns it on Yudhishthira himself. Then someone nobody expects speaks up, a young man from the other side of the family. Two answers to Draupadi's question: one made of fury, one made of reasons.
screen: `TWO VOICES BREAK THE SILENCE.` → `ONE WITH FURY.` → `ONE WITH REASONS.`

segments.voice: Bhima's words are shocking. Gamblers, he says, don't stake even the women kept in their houses. Then: Sahadeva, bring fire, and I'll burn this brother's arms. It's the rage of someone who loves his brother and can't bear what he's done. Arjuna stops him: our enemies want exactly this, to see us turn on our eldest. And Bhima holds back. Then Vikarna speaks. He's one of Duryodhana's own brothers, a Kaurava, and he stands up in his family's hall and says: answer her. Nobody does. So he answers it himself, with reasons. Kings, he says, are prone to certain vices: hunting, drinking, dice, and too much pleasure. A man in their grip acts without judgment. Yudhishthira staked Draupadi in the grip of the game, at Shakuni's prompting, after he had already lost himself. And she's the wife of all five brothers, not his alone. For these reasons, Vikarna says, she was not won. The hall erupts, cheering him and blaming Shakuni. Notice who gave the answer: not an elder, not a Pandava, but a younger brother of the winning side. That's a real Hindu teaching, and the epics keep coming back to it. Dharma isn't loyalty to your own team. It binds you even against your own family. The tradition honors the ones who said so: Vikarna here, and in the Ramayana, Vibhishana, who told his own brother Ravana to give Sita back. And see how Vikarna does it: not with Bhima's fire, but with reasons, out loud, in his own family's hall.

Shape it the way Vikarna did, a reason instead of a shout. Many Hindus make a sankalpa, a small resolve, before their home shrine. If you pray, make yours there and ask for courage; if you don't, write the sentence down and keep it.

773.hook: Karna answers Vikarna, an order is given, the cloth keeps coming, and a tradition answers Karna

773.howItsDone: The unending cloth is told in homes, sung in devotional songs and danced on stage, where devotees see Krishna's protection; in Tamil Nadu, Draupadi is worshiped as Draupadi Amman, with festivals that act out the epic and end in a fire-walk.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vikarna, a Kaurava, answered Draupadi's question with reasons. Dharma comes before your own side.

The cheering for Vikarna doesn't last. Karna rises, Duryodhana's friend, and he's angry. He doesn't simply shout, the way Bhima did a moment ago. He comes at it with arguments of his own, point after point, aimed straight at the young man who dared to speak for her. Then, briefly and with care: what the hall tries to do to Draupadi, and what it can't do.
screen: `THE CHEERING DOESN'T LAST.` → `KARNA RISES.` → `WHAT THE HALL CAN'T DO.`

segments.voice: Karna tells Vikarna he's a boy talking like an elder. The elders have kept quiet, he says, so they must think she was won. Yudhishthira staked everything he owned, and she was part of everything. Then Karna says cruel things about Draupadi herself, meant to make her less than a wife, and i won't repeat them. He orders Duhshasana: take the Pandavas' upper garments, and hers too. Duhshasana seizes Draupadi's garment and pulls. She cries out, in Ganguli's telling to Krishna, by name. And as he pulls, another garment appears beneath, and another, of many colors, until a great heap lies on the floor and he sinks down, worn out and ashamed. Bhima, shaking with rage, swears before everyone that one day, in battle, he'll drink Duhshasana's blood. Karna tried to make Draupadi less than a person who could ask a question. Here is how Hindu tradition answered him. In Tamil Nadu, Draupadi is worshiped as a goddess, Draupadi Amman, in temples of her own. At her festivals the Mahabharata is acted out as village theater, this hall included, and the festival often ends with devotees walking across hot coals in her honor. Tamil communities as far away as Singapore keep that fire-walk too. That's the teaching: in this tradition, shame doesn't get the last word. The woman they dragged into the hall is the goddess people walk through fire for.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who's been shamed in public lately: in a hallway, a group chat, the news. Many Hindus light a small lamp, a diya, as a prayer for someone. If you can, light one, or a candle, or simply picture its flame, and hold that person in its light, not smaller but honored. If you pray, ask that they be covered and kept; if you don't, wish them their dignity back.

774.title: Vidura's story of Prahlada
774.hook: Vidura tells the hall of Prahlada, a father who judged against his own son rather than answer falsely
774.carry: elders who won't speak dharma aren't elders
774.howItsDone: Vidura's story of Prahlada's honest verdict is retold as a lesson about speaking truly in a council, and his verse that they aren't elders who don't speak dharma is often quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday Draupadi's question met Karna's scorn, and the cloth kept coming. Draupadi Amman: the one they shamed is worshiped.

The heap of cloth lies on the floor. The hall is shaken, and still no one has answered Draupadi. So Vidura stands, and instead of an argument, he tells an old story. It's about a judge asked to decide a case in which his own son was one of the two sides. The question for him was simple and terrible: will you tell the truth if it costs your own child?
screen: `STILL NO ONE HAS ANSWERED.` → `VIDURA TELLS A STORY.` → `A JUDGE, AND HIS OWN SON.`

segments.voice: Vidura begins with the hall. Draupadi has asked a question, he says, and it must be answered. Someone who knows the answer and stays silent shares in the wrong, and so does someone who answers falsely. Then the story. Two young men, Virochana, Prahlada's son, and Sudhanvan, a Brahmin's son, quarreled over which of them was greater, and staked their lives on it. They went to Prahlada, Virochana's own father, to judge. Sudhanvan warned him: answer falsely, or not at all, and you'll suffer for it. Prahlada went to the sage Kashyapa and asked what becomes of one who won't answer, or answers wrongly. A heavy burden of wrong, Kashyapa said. So Prahlada gave his verdict, against his own son: Sudhanvan is the greater, and his father is greater than i am. And Sudhanvan, moved by that honesty, gave Virochana's life back. Then Vidura turns to the kings: you've heard it. Now answer her. The telling says the kings said nothing at all. Vidura keeps this teaching all through the epic. Years later, counseling the blind king, he tells the same story of Prahlada again, and a verse from that counsel is often quoted by Hindus: it's no assembly if there are no elders in it; and they aren't elders if they don't speak dharma. That's the teaching. In Hindu homes, elders are honored, feet touched, first served, because an elder is meant to say what's right when it's hard. The silent kings in this hall had the age and the rank, and gave up the very thing that made them elders.

If you pray, add a request for the courage to speak dharma when it matters; if you don't, simply decide that you'll speak up kindly.

775.title: Two boons, and no third
775.hook: the question is never answered, but omens frighten the blind king, and Draupadi frees her husbands with two boons
775.carry: lobha: wanting without end wears dharma away
775.tomorrow: Why go back for one more game?
775.howItsDone: Draupadi's two boons and her refusal of a third are retold as a picture of dignity and of lobha, greed, refused; in parts of south India Draupadi herself is honored as a goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vidura told of Prahlada, and still no one answered Draupadi. Elders who won't speak dharma aren't elders.

Draupadi asks one more time. In the telling, she says she has been dragged here and wronged before everyone, and still no one has spoken. Then, once more: am I a slave, or free? Say it, and I'll accept it. And this time something does answer, though not from the people in the hall. By the end of this long day, a blind king finally speaks.

Bhishma answers once more, and again he can't settle it: Yudhishthira alone, he says, should say whether she was won. Duryodhana, smiling, sets a trap: let the four younger brothers say Yudhishthira wasn't their master, and she'll be free. Before they answer, Duryodhana makes an insulting gesture toward Draupadi, and Bhima swears a second vow, against him. Arjuna answers the trap: he was our master when he staked us, but whose master was he once he'd lost himself? Then the sounds begin. A jackal howls in the chamber where the king's sacred fire is kept. Donkeys bray. Birds cry out. Gandhari and Vidura hear it and tell the blind king. And Dhritarashtra, frightened, finally acts. He rebukes his son and offers Draupadi a boon. She asks for Yudhishthira's freedom, so her son won't be called a slave's son. Granted. A second: that the other four go free, with their weapons and chariots. Granted. Then he offers a third, and Draupadi refuses. Greed, she says, wears away dharma. A woman of a warrior's house may ask two boons; her husbands, now free, can win the rest by their own deeds. That word is lobha, greed, and Hindu teaching counts it among the six inner enemies, beside desire and anger. Notice: asking wasn't the problem. Draupadi asked, and asked well, for exactly what freed the people she loved. Lobha is the wanting that never stops. She knew where enough was, and put the asking down.

776.title: Into the forest
776.hook: a second game, a stake of forest and hiding, and the people of the city follow the Pandavas out
776.carry: vanaprastha: the forest is for growing, not only loss
776.tomorrow: How do you feed guests with nothing?
776.howItsDone: The Vana Parva, the book of the forest, is read and retold for the many stories the Pandavas hear in exile; and the forest names a stage of Hindu life, vanaprastha, that many elders still speak of.

segments.voice: Yesterday Draupadi's question went unanswered, yet she asked two boons and refused a third. Lobha, wanting without end, wears dharma away.

The Pandavas set out for home, free, with their weapons and their chariots. They don't get far. Back in the hall, Duryodhana is already talking to his father. In the telling, a messenger catches up with Yudhishthira on the road and calls him back for one more game. The stake this time isn't gold or brothers. It's exile. The book of the hall closes, and the long book of the forest, the Vana, begins.
screen: `FREE, AND ON THE ROAD.` → `CALLED BACK FOR ONE MORE GAME.` → `THE BOOK OF THE FOREST BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira hears the summons, and turns around. Good and evil come to beings as the creator ordains, he says, and summoned by the old king, he won't refuse. The terms: whoever loses goes into the forest for twelve years, in deer skins, then spends a thirteenth year in some town without being recognized. If they're found in that year, it begins again. Shakuni throws, and wins. As the Pandavas leave, Vidura describes each of them to the blind king. Yudhishthira covers his face. Bhima looks at his great arms. Arjuna scatters sand as he walks. The twins smear themselves with dust. Draupadi goes weeping, her face hidden by her loosened hair. Kunti stays behind in Vidura's house. Then, as the Vana Parva opens, the people of the city follow them out, and Yudhishthira has to ask them, gently, to go home. Vana means forest. For the Pandavas it's loss. But in Hindu teaching the forest is never only loss. It's where the rishis lived and taught; some of the old Vedic texts are called the Aranyakas, the forest books. And a stage of life is named for it. Hindu tradition describes four stages, the ashramas: student, householder, then vanaprastha, the forest-dweller, when a person steps back from running the house and turns toward God, and last, sannyasa, letting go of everything. Few people move to a real forest now. But many Hindu grandparents still speak of their vanaprastha years: giving things away, more prayer, more temple, pilgrimage. The Pandavas didn't choose their forest. It will still be where they hear more teaching than anywhere else.

777.title: The sun's gift in the forest
777.hook: the Brahmanas follow the exiles into the forest, and Yudhishthira has nothing to feed them until the sun gives a vessel
777.carry: surya: the sun who ripens food for all
777.tomorrow: Where was Krishna during the game?
777.howItsDone: The story of Surya's vessel is retold in Hindu storytelling, and the sun's place as the giver of food lives on in the daily offering of water, arghya, and in the festival of Chhath.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Pandavas walked into the forest. In Hindu teaching the forest is for growing, not only loss: vanaprastha.

A crowd is following the exiles. The Pandavas have lost their kingdom, their wealth and their palace, and still a company of Brahmanas keeps walking behind them into the trees, refusing to turn back. That night, by the water, Yudhishthira lies awake with a very practical problem. He can't send his guests away; a host doesn't do that. And he has nothing to feed them. How do you feed the people who chose to stay?
screen: `A CROWD FOLLOWS THE EXILES.` → `NOTHING TO FEED THEM.` → `HOW DO YOU FEED THOSE WHO STAY?`

segments.voice: The family priest, Dhaumya, gives him counsel. Turn to Surya, the sun, he says: it is the sun that ripens what the earth gives, and so feeds every creature. In Ganguli's telling, Dhaumya teaches him a hundred and eight names of the sun. So Yudhishthira purifies himself with water, and praises the sun. And Surya appears, blazing, with a gift: a copper vessel. Whatever is cooked in your kitchen, the sun tells him, won't run out for your guests, as long as Draupadi hasn't yet eaten. So the forest household finds its shape. Draupadi serves the Brahmanas first, then her husbands, and only after everyone has eaten does she eat, and the vessel is done for the day. Here's the teaching under the story. Hindus honor the sun as a god, Surya, because every meal starts with him: he ripens the grain. That's why so many Hindus still greet the morning sun by pouring out a little water toward it, an offering called arghya, often standing in a river. And at the autumn festival of Chhath, families from Bihar and nearby regions fast, then stand in rivers and lakes at sunset and again at sunrise, offering to the sun in thanks for harvest and life. When the Pandavas had lost everything, they started by thanking the one who feeds every creature. Their camp didn't get a palace back. It got a table.

If you pray, say it and give thanks for the food today will bring; if you don't, pour the water on a plant tomorrow and think of the sun inside your next meal.
